name: PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Tambangraya Megah: a net-cash, high-CV Kalimantan producer whose dividend no longer covers the tape premium
frontmatter.summary: ITM sells high-CV Kalimantan coal at a fixed-price-driven discount to the Newcastle marker, runs net cash and pays a variable dividend. This update marks the FY2026 interim dividend: declared well above last year's and a larger share of first-half profit, it lifts the payout input to the top of the LK's disclosed payout record and the dividend leg with it, but the target stays below the tape and the total return negative. The rating is unchanged.
thesis: The current year's realised price is measured on the six-month actual, not read off a stable-ratio assumption: two-thirds of the sales book is fixed-price, so a rising marker is not passed through at the prior-year ratio [S2, F26].

Volume is the company's own plan, not our call: the current-year line sits inside the published indicative sales range, is held near the top of it through the near term and then eases onto a flat line, because the stated reserve base supports well over a decade at that rate and nothing in the mine plan sources a fade [S2, S3].

The balance sheet is the hinge: net cash, a small debt line and a sized buyback programme mean the dividend and the capital return, not the finite-life DCF, are what the market is capitalising, and the declared FY2026 interim sits above the prior year and takes the payout to the top of the LK's disclosed payout record [S0, S7, S8].

Costs follow the record rather than a single quarter: the strip ratio is held at the last complete half-year actual against the audited full years, the purchased-coal book is re-based to the gap between the sales target and the production target, and the effective tax rate is the LK's own three-year average, reconciled line by line in the financial section [S2, S3].

The scenarios mirror on the benchmark and the domestic take, with the royalty charged in the bear; the one-stop export channel carries no disclosed fee or realised-price effect, so it is a monitored transition rather than a priced shock. The bear sizes its volume clip to the Indominco concession and the bull cannot mirror it upward because the work-plan quota caps output [S2, S6].

blocks.text: **What changed (9 November 2026).** The board declared the FY2026 interim at Rp1,191 a share, cum 10 November 2026, against Rp738 a year earlier [S8, F46, F47]. It absorbs a larger share of first-half profit, supporting the top rather than the floor of the LK's disclosed payout record: the input moves to 65.0% on a leg carrying 15.0% of the value [S8, S0, S3]. The interim is about half our modelled full-year DPS of Rp2,681 [S8, S0].

The attribution, leg by leg: the payout step lifted the dividend leg; the strip re-basing and the tax rate re-based to the LK's three-year average lifted the primary DCF; and the EV/EBITDA weight came down to 15.0% because that leg sits 40.7% above the DCF [S0, S2, S3]. After the DPS deduction the news is worth only a small part of the target. The buyback cash remains a negative bridge item and the proforma count of 1,026m is on every leg [S7, F43, F45].

We keep PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp21,982** against Rp24,825: a total return of **-0.7%**, with the dividend no longer enough to carry the equity past the tape. ITM is Banpu's Indonesian thermal-coal arm: four CCoW concessions in East and Central Kalimantan plus IUPs, high-CV product, net cash [S2, S3].

Our through-cycle NAV - a full-life DCF to reserve depletion with no terminal value - is **Rp20,732**, below the tape: the deck's long-run marker mean-reverts below spot and we do not capitalise the war premium. The dividend method lifts the blend to **Rp23,230** and EV/EBITDA sits at Rp29,171, 40.7% above the DCF, both below the price [S0].

The variant view: the tape implies the benchmark holds near **US$126/t**, a factor of 1.1 on the FY2027E marker [S0] - too generous on price, not too harsh on volume. The benchmark, the RKAB quota and the domestic take move the value [S2, S3].

PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal producer, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007 and now a subsidiary of Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., which holds 65.1% indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the balance in public hands and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. It reports and sells in US dollars and employs 1,609.0 people [S0].

The business is one commodity across four CCoW concessions - Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I, East Kalimantan), Trubaindo (Gen II), Bharinto Ekatama (Gen III) and Jorong Barutama Greston (Gen II, South Kalimantan) - plus four IUPs (Graha Panca Karsa, Tepian Indah Sukses, Nusa Persada Resources, Kitadin) [S3]. The mix skews to the higher grades, Imm, Tcm and Bek, while Jbg, Gpk and Npr sit lower, so the realised price keys off Newcastle and HBA rather than the low-grade ICI indices [S2].

Adjacent businesses are small: coal trading, mining contractor and port services, a barge port for the Melak cluster, a rooftop-solar arm, and a mineral-sector vehicle stood up in October 2026 [S2, S3, S4]. The vehicle holds a minority stake in the listed laterite-nickel miner PT Adhi Kartiko Pratama, carried at nil because no archived filing discloses its cost, value or segment profit, and its expansion capex is excluded while no return is credited [S2, S3, S4].

The competitive position is a mid-sized, high-grade, low-cost Indonesian producer: a price-taker whose unit cost sits inside the peer band [S3]. Its reserve base was 382 Mt at end-2025 [S3, F11], a reserve life of roughly seventeen years on the 22.9 Mt production plan, the life the DCF runs to depletion. The company announced a buyback of up to IDR2.31tn on 4 November 2026, running three months [S7, F41]; the nearest expiry is the Indominco concession in March 2028, also the largest production unit [S2].

Thermal coal is a cyclical, dollar-priced, policy-shaped commodity, and the deck frames it that way: the Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg marker is the price series, the DMO cap is the administered ceiling on domestic power tonnes, and the marginal Indonesian tonne clears near its long-run marker once the war premium fades [S0]. Our read is that supply discipline, not demand growth, has held the price up: RKAB uncertainty and higher domestic obligations constrain Indonesian supply, with Chinese output and Indian import substitution the demand-side dampeners [S2].

Regulation is the swing factor. Coal sits under the RKAB annual work-plan approval, which sets permitted volume, and under the domestic market obligation that reserves a share of output for the national power market at the administered cap [S2, S3]. The royalty regime depends on the licence: the CCoW mines pay a contract-specific rate and the IUPs the lower schedule, and the group booked 220 USD m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m, below the contract headline [S3].

The newest layer is the export channel: from 1 January 2027 strategic-resource exports, coal included, must be handled by the state export company PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026, and the coal Eksportir Terdaftar licence is valid only to 31 December 2026 [S6]. The export base is 19.2 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F21]. The exposure is process rather than price - nothing reported sets a fee or a different realised price - so neither scenario shocks it and it stays a shipment-timing risk [S6].

The moat is grade and cost position rather than scale: a high-CV product at a unit cost inside the peer band is what survives a trough [S3]. Pricing power is nil on the marker and real on the mix, but the mix cuts both ways: because 67.0% of current-year sales are fixed-price and only a quarter indexed, a marker move reaches the realised price with a lag and the ratio falls when the marker rises [S2, F26]. On the five forces, supplier power is moderate, buyer power high, substitutes real but slow [S2], new entrants gated by permits and the RKAB, and rivalry disciplined by the same regime.

The five-year record is a classic coal cycle. Revenue ran at US$3,636.2m in the peak year and fell to US$2,374.3m, US$2,304.5m and US$1,881.1m [S0, S3]. The compression is entirely price: volumes were steady at 24.0 and 24.7 of sales tonnage [S3], while the realised price fell from 95.7 to 76.0 and net profit to parent to US$190.9m [S5, S0].

Our forecast rebuilds the same way: revenue is volume times a capped realised price, with volume the company's own current-year range held flat [S2] and the realised price the deck's Newcastle marker times a ratio fitted on the six-month actual for the current year and the last two completed years thereafter as the fixed book rolls off [S5, S2]. First-forecast-year revenue is US$2,203.5m at 81.0, above last year's 76.0, and EBITDA of US$321.0m reproduces the last actual year on more tonnes, the deeper strip and larger purchased book absorbing the price gain [S0, S2 p.21].

Costs are where caution creeps in, and we have taken it out. Cash cost per tonne is the strip ratio times the mining cost per cubic metre, backed out of the LK's cost-of-revenue note, plus a residual for hauling, barging, processing and the purchased-coal book [S3]. The strip ratio is held at 10.3 from the first full forecast year - the first-half actual [S2, F18], not the deeper single-quarter guidance the previous edition extrapolated over the horizon - against the FY2025A audited 9.4x [S3, F7], the right comparison because the LK prices stripping against a pit-life ratio [S3 p.128, p.335]. The purchased book is rebuilt, and royalty is the booked effective rate with SG&A held at the last actual's share of revenue [S3].

Tax is the rate the LK books, not the pack's three-year average of 25.0%: FY2025 tax was US$92.5m on pre-tax profit of US$287.2m, against US$119.2m on US$494.8m and US$144.5m on US$644.1m [S3 p.17]. The last year is not structural: the statutory charge of 63.2 US$m is lifted by a 23.9 US$m prior-year sales adjustment under PP No. 15/2022 and PP No. 18/2025 and by 13.3 US$m of unrecognised deferred tax assets [S3 p.370]. We carry the three-year average; at the FY2025 rate the total return stays inside the HOLD band, so that year does not flip the rating.

We restate depreciation rather than model around it: the pack's prior-year figure is a stub because the cash-flow statement uses the direct method, so we take the LK's own charge for the last two years and let the engine rebuild history [S3]. The line is property, plant and equipment depreciation charged to cost of revenue; right-of-use depreciation is an operating cost inside the selling and G&A lines, which is why our last-year EBITDA sits below the company's presented 343 USD m: the company adds back total D&A, including 36.9 USD m of right-of-use depreciation [S5 p.23, S3]. The 35.5 USD m of cash lease payments bears the treatment out [S3].

The bridge uses the company's own 30 June 2026 balance sheet: cash of 738 USD m against borrowings of 18.0 USD m, a net-cash position [S2]. The pack's larger debt line is total debt including lease liabilities, the lease component a derived residual [S2, S3 p.142]. Capex is sustaining spend per tonne, held flat in nominal terms, and reconciles as 79.0 USD m of PPE purchases plus 40.7 USD m of deferred exploration and development [S3]. Working capital is held at the historical ratio and no new borrowing is assumed [S0, S2].

Capital allocation runs three ways: sustaining capex, the FY2026 interim of Rp1,191 a share declared cum 10 November 2026, and the buyback of up to IDR2.31tn [S8, S7, F41]. On the modelled payout the year carries Rp2,681 a share, so the final payment is the balance [S8, S0]. Both returns come from net cash rather than new debt, and the dividend is a board decision, not a formula [S3, S8].

Earnings quality. ITM is clean. Operating cash flow of 285.5 US$m exceeded net profit of US$194.7m, so the accruals ratio is negative and earnings are cash-backed [S0, S3]. There is no special-notation or special-board flag and the LK is audited and unqualified [S3]. Related-party sales were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. The buyback spends cash that leaves the bridge as a negative item and cuts the count to 1,026m, an eight per cent reduction in the share-change input [S7, F43]; because the purchase price is above our through-cycle value the net per-share effect is negative. The 20.0% cap includes existing treasury shares, and there is no rights-issue or discounted-placement pattern [S2, S3]. One optics-class flag: the variable dividend is a board decision at the top of the LK's payout record [S0, S3, S8].

We value ITM on the house method for commodity producers: a through-cycle DCF over the mine's economic life as the primary method, an EV/EBITDA and a dividend-capacity cross-check, weighted **70.0%**, **15.0%** and **15.0%** [S0]. The fit is a finite, price-taking cash-flow stream, and a cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs: risk-free 4.9%, mature-market premium 4.2%, country premium 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 0.80 lifting to 0.81 at the statutory tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of **10.8%** and a WACC of **10.7%** [S0]. The 0.5% premium is for control-structure opacity: the Group's own assets are unpledged and the bank facilities unsecured [S3 p.382, p.395], but nothing discloses whether the controlling block is pledged, and the previous edition's clean claim is withdrawn [S3].

The primary method gives **Rp20,732** per share, below the tape, and the reason is the deck, not the company: the long-run marker is flat in real terms and well below spot, the war premium is a cycle position, and the realised price is a fraction of the marker [S0]. The DCF runs on sales tonnes, so the purchased book draws down the reserve statement and biases the NAV down slightly. Free cash flow is negative in the late reserve years as the strip bites, but the working-capital release offsets it, so the tail adds under one per cent to the NAV. Net of the small debt line, the enterprise value is 597.1 [S0].

The cross-checks diverge, and that is the point. EV/EBITDA gives **Rp29,171**, 40.7% above the primary, because the multiple blends peers trading on a war-premium cash flow [S0]. The dividend method gives **Rp23,230**, 12.0% above, because it capitalises the modelled cash return rather than the finite-life value [S0]. It capitalises the dividend at **11.5%** against a forward yield of 10.8% [S0], at a payout of 65.0% taken at the top of the LK's record on the declared interim [S8, S3]. That makes it the most generous leg and the one we would defend least [S3, S8]. The multiple blends the peer median with ITM's own trailing-yield average, and on that own-history half alone the EV/EBITDA leg would sit only around a third above the DCF [S0].

The red team is right that a cross-check this far above the primary cannot carry a quarter of the value: the weight is cut to 15.0% and the primary raised to 70.0%, so the target is predominantly the through-cycle NAV [S0]. The buyback is in the arithmetic on every leg and on one share count: its cash cost enters `valuation.bridge` as a negative item and the proforma count of 1,026m shares is used in the forecast share line and the market count [S7, F41, F43, F45]. The net effect is negative because the purchase price is above our through-cycle value. On the dividend leg the cash is not deducted twice: a per-share dividend capitalisation values a flow, and the DPS is already struck on the post-buyback count. The bridge assumes full execution of the maximum budget, so a partial programme would leave the target several hundred rupiah a share higher [S7, F41].

What the benchmark is worth at the spot: the reviewed spot is US$150/t against a FY2027E marker of US$118/t, and the sensitivity table's outer price column is the nearest grid point [S0]. The tape implies only **US$126/t**, a factor of 1.1 on the marker, so the market is not paying for the spot either [S0]. We present the spot value as an upper bound - the reserve's worth if the war premium is permanent - and keep the base on the deck's marker; the bull is set a seventh above the deck rather than at spot, which would price the premium as permanent.

What the price implies: run the DCF backwards and the tape requires the Newcastle benchmark near **US$126/t**, a factor of 1.1 on the FY2027E marker [S0]. That embeds the war premium persisting, a low-yield dividend capitalisation and no policy surprise. We do not think the premium persists, and our target sits below the price because the dividend no longer covers the gap between the tape and the finite-life value.

The downside risks. **Regulatory** (medium likelihood, high impact): the RKAB cycle sets the volume line and the domestic obligation diverts tonnes to the capped power market [S2]. **Concession** (medium, high): Indominco expires in March 2028 and is the largest single production unit with the thinnest reserve base [S2]. **Export channel** (medium, medium): from 1 January 2027 coal may be exported only through PT DSI, and APBI warns an unprepared transition could stall shipments [S6]; we size it rather than dismiss it, because exports are 19.2 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F21], so a quarter's clearance gap defers roughly a fifth of a year's export tonnes - a late receivable, not a revenue loss, the true cost below the bear's volume clip [S3, F21, S6]. **Governance** (low, medium): related-party flows are small, but whether the controlling block is pledged is not disclosed [S3]. **Macro** (medium, high): the complex carries a war premium and the deck sees the long-run marker well below spot [S0]. **FX** (low, medium): dollar revenue against a partly rupiah cost base [S3]. **Operational** (medium, medium): the mine plan raises the strip ratio as pits deepen [S2]. **Liquidity** (low, low): the shares are liquid and the free float roughly a third [S0, S3]. **Capital allocation** (medium, medium): the buyback of up to IDR2.31tn runs from 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027 from internal cash, and the shares trade above our through-cycle value, so execution transfers value between holders [S7, F41].

Our scenarios are mirrored on the benchmark, and we have not stacked the bear. The price shocks are a symmetric fourteen per cent either side of the deck's path across the whole forecast, so the year elapsed at the reviewed spot is charged in the bear as well as credited in the bull. The bear adds three things: it sizes its volume clip to the Indominco concession, where the mine is 7.1 Mt of the 22.9 Mt plan, holds 31.0 Mt of reserves and expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume at a present-value equivalent; it charges the royalty an onerous renewal would lift toward the contract headline, unmirrored in the bull because no sourced mechanism lets the booked rate fall [S3]; and it takes the payout back to the FY2025 LK's own floor, unmirrored because the base already sits at the top of the disclosed record [S3 p.157]. The bull mirrors the benchmark and runs volume at the top of the guided range, and cannot mirror the volume cut upward because the work-plan quota caps output [S2, F15].

On those shocks the bear is **Rp13,366**, the bull **Rp32,418** and the base **Rp22,103**, at probabilities of 0.25, 0.55 and 0.20 [S0]. The bull carries a smaller weight because its volume upside is capped by guidance while the bear's Indominco mechanism is a live concession expiry; the price legs are mirrored, and the macro desk is neutral on thermal coal [S0].

The probability-weighted target of Rp21,982 sits below Rp24,825 and the total return is -0.7% - inside the band, but only just - so the HOLD rests on the cash return rather than on the value of the mine. Because the rating sits near zero, signposts matter: an RKAB outcome below the indicative range; a domestic obligation above the current share; whether the export channel clears coal without a shipment gap in early 2027 [S6]; a sustained marker move either side of the deck path; the Indominco extension terms; and a buyback executed below our through-cycle value. Any two moving the wrong way take the total return through the REDUCE band.

Ownership is straightforward. Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. holds 65.1% indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. The register shows the Group's own assets unencumbered and the bank facilities without collateral [S3 p.382, p.395]; it does not show whether the controlling block is pledged, because no share-register or pledge disclosure appears in any archived filing, and we carry a small cost-of-equity premium for that gap instead of asserting the clean answer [S3]. The audit is unqualified [S3].

Related-party coal sales were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. We found no discounted placement, serial rights issue or auditor down-tier change. The buyback of up to IDR2.31tn runs to 4 February 2027, is capped at 20.0% of paid-up capital and is a capital return we do not value because the shares trade above our through-cycle value [S7, F41, F44].

The dividend record is variable: the LK shows a large share of each year's profit distributed with no formulaic floor [S0, S3]. We carry 65.0%, the top of the record, because the declared interim of Rp1,191 absorbs a larger share of first-half profit than the prior-year Rp738, evidence for the top rather than the floor [S8, F46, F47]. The interim is funded from internal cash alongside the buyback, so neither return is borrowed [S8, S7]. On ESG, the group reports third-party scores but names neither the score nor a verifiable median, so we claim no relative position; disclosed are biodiesel and grid-power emissions work and post-mining rehabilitation [S2]. A thermal-coal producer carries an unavoidable transition discount; what is controllable is capital discipline and reclamation, and both read as adequate [S2, S3].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 interim, cum 10 November with payment later in the month [S8], the third-quarter operational release, the FY2027 RKAB approval that sets next year's volume, the 1 January 2027 switch to the state export channel [S6], and the annual general meeting that declares the final dividend and may renew the buyback authority [S2, S3].

Between updates we monitor sales volume against the range; the realised price against the deck; strip ratio and unit cash cost against the mine plan; the booked royalty rate, the cleanest early signal of a regime change; net debt; the payout ratio, the market's anchor; and, from January 2027, the export share cleared through the state exporter [S0, S3, S6]. The royalty rate and the reserve statement matter most, because either would re-price the model or change how long it runs. The fixed-price book means the realisation ratio moves with the marker, so a few points is the assumption most likely to be wrong.

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the benchmark 14% below the deck's path across the forecast - the exact mirror of the bull's 14% above it - a demand-led trough through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names as the level at which marginal Indonesian supply clears. The whole-forecast multiplier is 0.86 rather than a from-FY2027 step, so the year already three-quarters elapsed at the reviewed spot is charged too; that is the harsher reading and it keeps the shock mirrored rather than asymmetric. The volume shock is now sized to the Indominco Mandiri concession, not a generic clip: IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.9 Mt top of the FY26 production plan [S2, F27, F28], holds only 31 Mt of reserves [S2, F29] and its CCoW Gen I expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume; the engine applies shocks to the whole forecast, so the banked clip is the PV-equivalent loss across the horizon. The government also raises the share of tonnes diverted to the capped domestic power market. The one-stop export transition (PP No. 24/2026, state exporter PT DSI from January 2027 [S6]) is NOT shocked as a separate volume line: a quarter's shipment gap on the export book defers rather than destroys tonnes (the coal stays in stock and the sale moves), and the bear's 0.78 volume multiplier - a permanent loss of a fifth of the mined book - is already several times the PV cost of a three-month deferral, so charging both would double-count. The deferral's real cost is the working capital: a quarter of the 19.2 Mt export book at the realised price is roughly US$0.4bn of receivables-older inventory, which is inside the bear's volume and cost path and is stated as a dated sensitivity in Section 5. The equity now also carries the payout downside inside the probability set (C10): the bear takes the payout back to the FY2025 LK's own 60% record [S3, p.157], a step of a twentieth on the dividend leg, so the leg the analysis says it would defend least is the leg the bear actually tests. The renewal is CHARGED, not just described (round-2 C4): an IMM extension on onerous terms - a conversion or extension that lifts the booked royalty toward the 13.5% CCoW headline [S3] - is carried as a 1.8pp add to the booked 11.7% rate, which is the step from the group's blended rate to the contract headline on the 7.1 Mt IMM block. That is applied in the bear rather than the base because the extension decision is binary at March 2028 and no source prices a specific extension fee. No re-rating or required-return shock is taken.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus Indonesian RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 14% above the deck's path across the forecast - the exact mirror of the bear's 14% below - which puts the FY2027 marker at about US$135, and ITM's high-CV Kalimantan coals capture the premium in full. This is deliberately anchored on the reviewed spot rather than on a round number: the deck's reviewed spot is US$150.35 and its FY2027 marker US$118, so a bull that capitalised the spot as a permanent level would be a scarcity-scenario, not the most likely path; the 14% premium is what the model needs to carry today's print as the current year and still fade it, and the reverse DCF shows the tape itself implies only about 1.11x the deck [S0]. Section 4 states what the reserve is worth at the spot itself. The export-channel transition clears without a shipment gap, so it adds no shock; volumes run at the TOP of the company's own guided sales range (27.5 of a 27.2 Mt base), not above it, because no archived source quantifies Bunyut throughput or an NPR uplift; and the domestic-market take eases back as export economics improve. The volume asymmetry against the bear is deliberate and sourced: upside is capped by the RKAB and the company's own 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2, F15], so a symmetric three-tenths uplift is not physically available and the bull earns its return from price. The probability weight is cut to reflect the smaller volume upside. The royalty rate and the required return are NOT shocked: no sourced mechanism lets the booked royalty rate fall, and a bull that assumes a re-rating would be a defect. The buyback programme is a capital-return lever only if executed below our through-cycle value; the shares trade above it, so no buyback credit is taken and the programme is not shocked in either leg [S7, F41].

assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own published target, not our guess: the 2Q26 analyst presentation puts FY26 indicative coal sales at 26.9-27.5 Mt [S2, F15] against FY2025 actual sales of 24.7 Mt [S3, F1] and 6M26 sales of 12.3 Mt [S2]. The step-up is sourced and structural rather than a market call: sales run well above production (FY2026 production target is 22.0-22.9 Mt against a 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2]) because the group draws down ROM and stockpile inventory and resells purchased coal through its trading arm, so the FY2026 sales line is the company's, held near the midpoint. FY2027E-FY2030E are held broadly FLAT rather than faded: the 382 Mt reserve base [S3, F11] supports roughly fourteen years at this run-rate and nothing in the mine plan [S2] sources a decline, and the most-likely rule forbids an unsourced volume fade. The reserves cap in the template, not a stylised fade, is what ends the volume line.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: RE-BASED ON THE 6M26 ACTUAL, not on a lagged H1 ratio. FY2026E 0.614 is set so that the engine reproduces the company's own six-month realised price: at the deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker (US$137.0), 0.78 x 0.614 x 137.0 + 0.22 x 70.0 = US$81.0/t, which is exactly the 6M26 ASP [S2 p.21] (F16 is the 2Q26 print of US$82.7/t, not the six-month figure). The previous 0.655 was the raw H1 ratio (US$81.0 over the H1-2026 average of about US$128.9) applied to a full-year marker 6% above the H1 level, which implicitly required an H2 ASP step-up that the contract book does not support: 67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed [S2, F26], so only about a quarter of the book can respond to a rising marker within the year. Holding the current year at the six-month actual is the most-likely read, not a haircut: it is the last actual, and the fixed two-thirds is locked. FY2027E-FY2030E revert to 0.7167, the ratio fitted on the last two completed fiscal years (FY2025A ASP US$76.0/t [S5, F3] over the deck's US$108.4 = 0.701; FY2024A US$95.7/t [S5, F4] over US$136.1 = 0.703, lifted to 0.7167 for the 22% capped domestic share), because the fixed 2026 book rolls off and the two-actual level is the through-cycle anchor. ITM's realised price is structurally below the Newcastle 6,000 marker: the product is a blend of 5,600-6,200 kcal/kg GAR (IMM) and higher-CV TCM/BEK coals [S2, F17], a fifth of tonnes go to the domestic market at HBA/DMO-linked prices [S3, F12], and the method card has Indonesian coal key off HBA/ICI rather than Newcastle. The FY2025A calibration gate is answered in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda: it re-prices history at the FY2026E ratio, a forecast-year measurement, not a mis-specified cost base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: The company's own disclosed domestic share: 5.5 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in FY2025 went to the Indonesian domestic market [S3, F12], i.e. 22.3% of sales volume, and those tonnes settle at HBA/DMO-linked prices against the standing US$70/t power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). We hold 22% of tonnes under the cap rather than ramping it: the DMO is a fixed government share of production (25% of output for domestic supply), and ITM's disclosed domestic share has been stable, so a rising domestic take is a policy risk stated in §5 rather than a modelled drift. Capped tonnes receive min(cap, realised price), which bites hardest in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Carried as the PHYSICAL overburden-to-coal ratio (bcm/t) on the AADI/GEMS/BUMI peer convention, so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm is the mining block per tonne and is directly comparable with the other COAL names. RE-BASED ON THE COMPANY'S OWN 3Q26 GUIDES after the round-2 challenge (C5). The 6M26 group average of 10.3x [S2, F18] is an H1 number and the company has already guided the pits deeper for the second half: IMM 14.0x on 1.9 Mt, TCM 17.6x on 0.8 Mt and BEK 7.7x on 2.3 Mt in 3Q26 [S2 pp.17-18], which is 11.68x on a production-weighted basis across those three mines and about 10.9x once the remaining ~0.7 Mt at roughly 5x is added (0.7 x 5 = 3.5; (26.6 + 14.1 + 17.7 + 3.5) / 5.7 = 10.9x). FY2026E is therefore the volume-weighted blend of the two halves actually known: 12.3 Mt at the 6M26 actual 10.3x and the guided 14.9 Mt at 10.9x, i.e. (12.3 x 10.3 + 14.9 x 10.9) / 27.2 = 10.6x. FY2027E onward now holds 10.3x, the LAST COMPLETE HALF-YEAR ACTUAL, and not the 3Q26 guidance of 10.9x. The red team's challenge (C1) is right that one quarter is not a life-of-mine schedule: 10.9x is a single quarter measured on three mines (about 5.7 Mt of the group's roughly 7 Mt), the LK itself prices stripping against an ESTIMATED PIT-LIFE ratio and defers the excess rather than re-basing the reserve (S3 p.335), and the two audited full years print 10.0x in FY2024 and 9.4x in FY2025 (S3 p.128) - a sequence that rises and falls with pit depth, not a trend. The through-cycle actual is therefore 10.3x, the most recent complete measure and 0.9x above the FY2025 average, so the guided step is charged for the half year that printed it and no further. Because strip x cost_per_bcm is the mining block at US$2.81/bcm, every 1.0x is about US$2.8/t on 27 Mt; the 10.9x path the previous edition carried is shown as a sensitivity in Section 4 so the reader sees what the single-quarter assumption removes.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: The overburden-removal and coal-getting cost per bank cubic metre. Backed out of the LK's own cost-of-revenue note: mining costs of US$653.3m on 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] is US$26.45/t, and at the FY2025A strip ratio of 9.4x [S3, F7] that is US$2.81/bcm — inside the US$2.6-8.0/bcm band the peer COAL names book, which is the check that the axis means the same thing across the deck. It escalates with the USD deck thereafter rather than falling in real terms, because the company names rising diesel and contract-mining rates as the live cost pressure (the presentation shows fuel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 a year earlier [S2]) and nothing in the filings sources a real decline.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Residual per-tonne cash cost ex-royalty and ex-D&A. RECALIBRATED TO THE 6M26 ACTUAL after the round-2 challenge (C1): the round-1 US$20.7/t was a bottom-up build off the FY2025 cost note and left the FY2026E line below the run-rate the company has already printed. The reconstruction: 6M26 revenue of US$1,000m at an US$81.0 ASP on 12.3 Mt gave a company-basis EBITDA of US$181.2m [S2 p.25, p.21]; on the model's lease basis (right-of-use and other D&A in the cost lines, not added back) that is about US$156m, or US$12.7/t. In the second half the guided 10.9x strip (vs 10.3x in H1) adds about US$1.7/t of cost, so H2 runs near US$11.0/t on the same ASP, giving a full-year line of US$156m + 14.9 Mt x US$11.0 = about US$320m on 27.2 Mt (US$11.8/t). At the modelled 10.6x strip and US$2.81/bcm the mining block contributes US$31.6/t, leaving US$18.8/t here. This is the residual that reconciles the model to the last actual, and it is consistent with the LK note from which the round-1 build started: the FY2025 cost of revenue of US$1,398.3m [S0] less royalty of US$220.0m [S3, F10] less depreciation of US$26.9m [S3, F8] over 24.7 Mt is US$46.6/t ex-royalty ex-D&A, of which mining was US$653.3m [S3, F24] and purchased coal US$256.3m [S3, F23]; the lower residual is the part of the FY2025 build (haul, barge, salaries, forestry, repairs, fuel) that the 6M26 actual shows running below the FY2025 average once the mining block is priced at the current strip. FY2026 sales of 27.2 Mt against a 22.0-22.9 Mt production target [S2, F28] implies about 4.75 Mt of purchased coal, which sits in this residual. SG&A is NOT here: ITM's selling and administrative expenses run at 11.5% of revenue and the engine carries them in opex_pct. Escalated gently with services and labour inflation thereafter.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes, not the data pack. ITM's consolidated depreciation of property, plant and equipment charged to cost of revenue was US$26.86m in FY2025 and US$38.71m in FY2024 [S3, F8, F9]. The pack's FY2025A D&A of US$32.5m is in the right region but its FY2024A figure of US$1.3m is a stub, because the IDX cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and carries no D&A add-back — which is exactly the restatement the method card asks for. THE RIGHT-OF-USE TREATMENT IS DELIBERATE AND IS NOT AN OMISSION: ROU depreciation was US$36.9m in FY2025 (US$32.5m of it in selling expenses [S3, F32]) and the ROU asset balance rose from US$3.0m to US$47.1m as new vessel, port and mine leases were capitalised [S3, F38]. We do NOT add that back here: the leases are treated as an operating cost, the cost lines the unit build reconciles to already carry the ROU depreciation, and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] matches it. Adding ROU back to EBITDA/FCFF while also choosing to pay the lease cash out of the same cost base would double-count. This is why the model's FY2025A EBITDA (US$293.5m = operating income + PPE depreciation in cost of revenue) sits below the company's presented EBITDA of US$343.1m, which adds the total D&A of US$76.2m back [S5 p.23]: the difference is ROU depreciation plus the ~US$12m of other depreciation/amortisation that sits in the cost lines. Held at the FY2025A rate of US$1.09/t thereafter on the flat volume path.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capital only. The FY2025 capex of US$119.7m on the data pack reconciles to the LK cash-flow statement as US$79.0m of property, plant and equipment purchases plus US$40.7m of deferred exploration and development (the deferred-stripping build) [S3, F36, F37], i.e. US$4.85/t total. Both legs are sustaining-grade spend tied to the mine: the deferred stripping is a direct function of the strip ratio, and the Bunyut/solar/mineral spend disclosed in the annual report has no separable dollar figure and no material-commitment note [S3 p.151], so it cannot be quantified out. The per-tonne line is nevertheless set at US$4.00/t, not US$4.85/t, because the most recent run-rate is materially lower: 6M26 capex was US$21m against US$32m in 6M25 [S2 p.23], an annualised ~US$42m, so US$4.00/t already sits ABOVE the current run-rate and only below the prior-year average that carried a large deferred-stripping addition. The discretionary expansion projects are not charged separately (capex_other is nil) and are carried at nil symmetrically. Held FLAT in nominal terms thereafter; the most-likely rule holds costs at the last actual in real terms and nothing sources a real rise.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: EXCLUDED from FCFF after the round-1 challenge. The previous build charged the Bunyut port capacity works, the solar pipeline (152 MWp contracted, 86 MWp operating at 2Q26 [S2, F31]) and the new mineral-sector vehicle ITM Mineral Investama [S4] through free cash flow while setting other_revenue to zero and carrying the assets at nil - a one-sided cost. No archived filing discloses segment revenue or a project value for any of them, and the most-likely rule forbids inventing one, so the discretionary expansion spend is removed from the coal DCF and the optionality is carried at nil rather than charged and ignored. Sustaining capex continues to carry the mine's own spend, and the port and solar works that serve the Melak cluster sit inside the operating cost base the LK reports. A sourced revenue or project value would add value; none exists in the record, and the bull adds nothing here for the same reason.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company pays out a variable share of net profit — its stated policy is to distribute part of each year's profit as cash dividend after allowing for reserves and the development plan [S3]. The LK's own payout-ratio disclosure is the guide, not a DPS/EPS series: the FY2025 annual report's dividend table states a payout ratio of 60% for the latest year and 64% for the prior year [S3, p.157], and the AGMS minutes put the FY2024 distribution at 65% of that year's net profit and FY2023 at 65% [S3, p.171/179] — a 60-65% record. The DPS/EPS arithmetic the pack carries (Rp992 in FY2025, Rp2,983 in FY2024) misleads because the pack's DPS is the dividend PAID during the year against the prior year's profit, so it mixes the payment lag with the cycle. The FY2026 interim settles the level rather than the static 60% label: the board declared Rp1,191.09 per share (cum date 10 November 2026), which is about US$68m on the post-buyback count, or 64% of the first-half 2026 net profit to parent of US$106.0m and 30% of our full-year forecast; last year's interim of Rp738 was US$50.0m, 55% of first-half 2025 profit of US$91.0m [S8, S3, S0]. On the FY2025 interim-to-final split the year then lands near 66% of profit, and on an even split it lands on 60%; the LK's own record is 60-65% [S3, p.157]. We therefore carry 65%, the top of the disclosed record, which the declared interim supports, rather than the 60% floor used in earlier editions — modelling the bottom of a 60-65% record with no evidence for the floor was a haircut, not a base case. The dividend is the anchor IDX coal names trade on, so the payout is also the market's own capitalisation rate and is cross-checked against dividend-capacity yield in §4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary DCF runs to the end of the reserve life with no terminal value, so this scalar only feeds the EV/EBITDA and implied-multiple cross-checks. It is set at zero because a thermal-coal cash-flow stream should not carry perpetual real growth — the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker is flat in real terms at US$105/t [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: ITM's selling and general and administrative expenses were US$171m and US$45m in FY2025 [S3], 11.5% of net revenue, against US$178m and US$37m in FY2024, 9.3%. The step-up is structural (higher fuel and oil in selling, and rising mine-administration cost [S3]), so we hold the FY2025A level rather than the three-year average, which is pulled down by the FY2023 low cost base. Held flat thereafter in nominal terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The effective rate the LK books, not the 13.5% CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025 (11.7%) and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024 (11.3%) [S3, F10]. That blend is the contract rate on the four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM and JBG Gen II, BEK Gen III) with the far lower IUP schedule on the IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin), plus the fact that the resold purchased-coal book carries no royalty — which is why a flat 11.7%, not 13.5%, reproduces what the group actually pays. Double-count check: royalty is inside the reported cost of revenue, so the mining block and other_cost_unit are set EX-ROYALTY and the engine adds royalty back as a separate percentage of revenue, counting the line once.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a real and rising cost pressure — the presentation shows diesel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 in 6M25 and names rising diesel and global inflation as a cost driver [S2] — but most of ITM's hauling, barging and contract mining is bought at unit rates that already embed the contractor's own diesel, so only a minority of the cost base is directly exposed. We set 15% rather than the 30% template convention, and give the reason: the oil deck's long-run Brent is a seeded, war-premium value, and passing a perpetual war premium through mining costs while the coal deck mean-reverts toward US$105/t would manufacture a margin squeeze that neither deck asserts.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: The renewable and mining-services lines are immaterial next to the coal book (solar capacity of 152 MWp contracted at 2Q26 [S2]) and are carried inside the coal revenue build, so no separate other-revenue line is modelled.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Template constant 10%; the non-coal lines are immaterial to group value.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: ITM is in a net-cash position — cash of US$738m against BORROWINGS of US$18m at 30 June 2026, i.e. net cash of US$720m, with the company reporting net gearing of negative 37% and debt-to-equity of 0.01x [S2, F34, F35] — so no new borrowing is assumed. The data pack's US$804.0m cash / US$99.3m debt is NOT used: its debt line is total debt including roughly US$81m of lease liabilities, and that lease component is a DERIVED residual (the pack's US$99.339m less the company's US$18.0m borrowings), not a disclosed 30 June 2026 figure. The last disclosed lease liability was US$50.153m at 31 December 2025 (US$40.351m current plus US$9.802m non-current [S3 p.142]); the six-month increase is an inference from new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and the valuation does not depend on it. Its cash line does not tie to the company's interim disclosure (see section 3). Leases are treated as an operating cost, not as debt: the LK already charges US$36.9m of right-of-use depreciation through selling and G&A expenses [S3, F32], and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] shows the cost base pays for the leases, so deducting the lease liability from equity as well would count the same obligation twice. The buyback disclosed on 4 November 2026 is funded from internal cash [S7, F41].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: ITM's non-operating line is dominated by finance income on its large net-cash balance, which the engine computes separately via cash_yield; no separate non-operating items are assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: MODELLED ON THE DISCLOSED PROFORMA after the round-2 challenge (C2). The buyback disclosed on 4 November 2026 is sized at up to Rp2.311 trillion over 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027 [S7, F41], and the company's own proforma puts the count at 1,026m shares from 1,114m after full use of the budget, a 7.9% reduction [S7, F43]. Round 1 carried a zero share change on the argument that a buyback executed above through-cycle value is value-neutral per share; that is wrong, and the challenge is accepted. The per-share arithmetic: US$127.9m of cash (Rp2.311tn at Rp18,075/US$) leaves the company, the count falls 7.9%, and because the purchase price of about Rp26,261 is above the DCF value the cash spent per share retired exceeds the value of each share retired, so value per share FALLS. The engine carries both legs: the cash outflow as a negative bridge item and the count through this input. FY2026E is set at -0.079 and held flat thereafter, so the reduction is taken once rather than compounded. The 20% cap includes the existing 2.4% treasury position [S2], so the effective headroom for new purchases is smaller than the headline; partial execution would leave value per share between the pre-buyback figure and the modelled one.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history (S0): the three-year average of net working capital over revenue. ITM's working capital is thin and mostly inventory and prepaid taxes, so this is a small drag and is held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: RE-BASED FROM THE LK'S OWN TAX NOTE after the red team's challenge (C2), replacing the data pack's 26.2%: 24.98% is the three-year average of the rates the LK books, built from the five-year summary on S3 p.17 - FY2023 tax of US$144.492m on pre-tax profit of US$644.112m (22.4%), FY2024 US$119.220m on US$494.821m (24.1%) and FY2025 US$92.539m on US$287.214m (32.2%). The 32.2% is not a new structural rate and is not extrapolated: the rate reconciliation on S3 p.370 shows the statutory 22% charge of US$63.187m lifted by two items - a US$23.922m sales adjustment booked on the application of Government Regulations 15/2022 and 18/2025, 8.3pp of pre-tax profit, and US$13.294m of unrecognised deferred tax assets, 4.6pp - against a US$7.765m credit for final-taxed finance income and US$0.318m of non-deductible expenses. The regulation-driven sales adjustment is a catch-up on prior-year treatment (it was US$4.728m in FY2024) and is not carried forward; the unrecognised deferred tax assets are a cash cost that recurs, which is why the forward rate sits above the statutory 22% rather than at it. The three-year average therefore includes FY2025 in full and FY2023-24 at the rates actually paid. Section 3 states the target at the FY2025 actual rate as well, so the rating's exposure to this input is visible rather than asserted.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). With borrowings of only US$18m against US$738m of cash at 30 June 2026 [S2, F34, F35] the cost of debt is not a value driver and the default is carried unchanged. The pack's US$99.3m debt line includes lease liabilities and is not used here.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). ITM holds a large net-cash balance and earns finance income of about US$40m a year on it (S0, S3), consistent with a low-single-digit treasury yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): minority interests take a small share of net profit, consistent with the reported non-controlling interest balance and the 99.99% ownership of the producing subsidiaries [S2].

challenges.challenge: strip_ratio is 10.6x in FY2026E and 10.9x from FY2027E to FY2045E against FY2025A 9.4x [S3, F7] and 6M26 10.3x [S2, F18]. The basis derives 10.9x from one quarter's pit sequence (3Q26 IMM 14.0x, TCM 17.6x, BEK 7.7x) and then concedes the same 6M26 print shows 10.3x is 'partly a pit-sequencing effect' - yet the sequence is held for nineteen years. Because unit_cost = strip x cost_per_bcm, each 1.0x is roughly US$2.8/t on 27 Mt, making this the single largest lever in the DCF.
challenges.answer: Strip re-based from 10.9x (one quarter, three mines) to 10.3x, the last complete half-year actual, held from FY2027E; the LK prices stripping against an estimated pit-life ratio (S3 p.335) and the audited years print 9.4x in FY2025 and 10.0x in FY2024 (S3 p.128). The 10.9x path is disclosed as the sensitivity.

challenges.challenge: a.tax_rate is 26.2%, the engine default from the data pack. The model's own FY2025A shows tax 92.539 on PBT 287.214, 32.2%, and FY2024 shows 119.22 on 494.821, 24.1%. Section 3 calls this 'the one unhedged optimistic departure' but asserts it is 'not large enough to move the rating on its own'. The house bands (fund rules) put HOLD at -10 < TR < +10 and REDUCE from -10, and the TR is -8.8%, so 1.2pp of cushion remains; 6pp of effective tax on the model's own EBIT and EPS carries the target through REDUCE. The assertion is false on the house's own numbers.
challenges.answer: Tax re-based from the pack 26.2% to 24.98%, the three-year average of the LK own charges, FY2023-FY2025 from S3 p.17. The FY2025 32.2% is explained line by line from the p.370 reconciliation: statutory 22% charge 63.187m, plus a 23.922m PP 15/2022 and 18/2025 sales catch-up and 13.294m unrecognised DTA, less 7.765m final-tax credit. Re-running at the FY2025 rate leaves the total return inside the HOLD band, now stated in the financial section.

challenges.challenge: From 1 January 2027 coal may be exported only through PT DSI; the Eksportir Terdaftar licence lapses on 31 December 2026 and APBI says coal may not be exportable on that date [S6]. Exports are 19.2 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold, 77.7% of sales [S3, F21]. Neither the bear's four shocks (newc 0.91, volume 0.78, capped_share +0.08, royalty +0.018) nor any scenario carries a shipment gap; the report calls it process rather than price and gives it zero probability weight.
challenges.answer: The export cliff is quantified in Section 5: exports are 19.2 Mt of 24.7 Mt sold, so a quarter clearance gap defers a fifth of a year export tonnes - a working-capital carry, not a revenue loss, since the coal stays in stock and the sale moves. It sits inside the bear permanent 0.78 volume clip rather than as a fifth shock, because charging both double-counts (S6).

challenges.challenge: No NAV at spot is presented, though the method card's output contract requires one and the coal deck carries a reviewed spot of US$150.35 against an FY2027E marker of US$118. The bull shocks newc to 1.2x the deck from FY2027, about US$142, which is still below the spot it is meant to represent; the reverse DCF says the tape implies US$131, only 1.11x the deck. The reader cannot see what the reserve is worth at the price the deck actually prints today.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the reviewed spot (US$150.35) against the FY2027E marker (US$118.0), points the reader to the sensitivity outer price column as the nearest grid point, and uses the reverse DCF - the tape implies 126.2, only 1.07x the marker - to show the market is not paying the spot either. The bull is anchored to the spot logic at +14% and the reason it is not struck at the spot itself is stated (S0).

challenges.challenge: The dividend leg capitalises the post-buyback DPS (EPS on 1,035m shares, about 8.6% above the 1,123.9m base) at 11.542% with no deduction of the Rp2.311tn buyback cash; Section 4 states this explicitly ('the dividend leg earns the higher per-share payout on the same reduced count'). The DCF and EV/EBITDA legs both deduct the cash, and the EV/EBITDA leg divides by 1,026m while the DCF divides by 1,035.1m. The leg is inflated by the buyback's per-share effect and the three legs do not use one share count.
challenges.answer: The share count is now one number everywhere: the forecast share line lands on the 1,026m proforma count (share_change -8.709% on 1,123.9m) and the market count and all three valuation legs use 1,026m, ending the 1,035.1m vs 1,026m split. The buyback cash is not deducted again inside the dividend leg because a per-share dividend capitalisation values a flow, not a stock, and the DPS is already struck post-buyback; the interest foregone is immaterial (S7, F43).

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg (3.3446x, 25% weight) contributes about 36% of the pre-scenario value of Rp20,185 and sits 84.8% above the DCF, and the multiple fell from 3.6985x in the previous edition to 3.3446x between 6 and 9 November with no change to any assumption except payout - a market re-mark worth about Rp500 of target. Section 4 concedes the multiple 'blends names trading on a war-premium cash flow' yet keeps the 25% weight, so the target is partly a mark-to-market of peers rather than a through-cycle value.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA weight is cut from 25% to 15% and the primary DCF raised to 70%, so the target is predominantly the through-cycle NAV; the 41% divergence is disclosed in Section 4 with the own-history half of the blend shown, and the peer set is named. The multiple is no longer presented as a through-cycle value (S0).

challenges.challenge: ITM Mineral Investama (stood up October 2026), the 152 MWp contracted and 86 MWp operating solar book and the Bunyut port works are carried at nil ('optionality at nil') while their expansion capex is excluded. The method card says development projects are worth at least their sourced sunk capex until a sourced project value exists, never zero. The report's support is that no archived filing discloses a separable sunk capex [S2, S3, S4], which is a search claim, not a valuation.
challenges.answer: Section 1 and the post-balance-sheet review now cite the disclosure line by line: the AR reports renewable capacity (12.9 to 63.7 MWp, +50.8 MWp in 2025, S3 p.133) and describes the operator entities CPI and CMSA, but discloses no separable capex, segment revenue or project value for solar, Bunyut or ITM Mineral Investama, and the company reports no material capital commitments. The assets remain at nil with the absence sourced and expansion capex excluded symmetrically.

challenges.challenge: Sections 4 and 6 assert there is 'no controlling-stake pledge on the register' and 'no margin-call structure [S3]'.
